results.title: Neuroinflammation across the Spectrum of Neurodegenerative Diseases: Mechanisms and Therapeutic Frontiers | Neuroimmunomodulation | Karger Publishers
results.content: Rather than being a mere consequence of neuronal injury, inflammatory processes, mediated by microglia, astrocytes, peripheral immune cells, and a range of molecular mediators, actively influence disease onset, progression, and clinical manifestations. Neuroinflammation, broadly defined as the immune response of the central nervous system (CNS) to diverse physiological or pathological stimuli, has gained increasing recognition as a central player in the onset and progression of neurodegenerative diseases. In this review, we examine the role of neuroinflammation across a range of major neurodegenerative disorders, including Alzheimer’s disease (AD), Parkinson’s disease (PD), amyotrophic lateral sclerosis (ALS), Huntington’s disease (HD), and multiple sclerosis (MS). We then explore disease-specific profiles of neuroinflammation, emphasizing how genetic, environmental, and systemic factors shape immune responses within distinct neurodegenerative contexts. The activation of microglia in neurodegenerative diseases is governed by a diverse array of receptor-mediated signaling pathways that orchestrate their functional states and responses to pathological stimuli. results.title: Mechanisms of microglia-mediated synapse turnover and synaptogenesis - ScienceDirect
results.content: Microglia shape synaptic connections among neurons of the central nervous system (CNS) during development and adulthood. In this review, the actions by which they facilitate pruning, refinement, and new synaptic development throughout the lifespan are considered, along with the molecular mechanisms by which neurons and microglia communicate to guide these actions. Microglia survey neuronal activity and selectively modify synaptic connections at the level of individual dendrites and synapses. Growth and elimination of synapses during development is dependent on signals from neurons as well as glial cells such as astrocytes, the primary structure and support macroglia cells of the CNS, and microglia, the primary macrophages of the CNS (Abraham et al., 2002, Thion et al., 2018). This review will discuss recent evidence that microglia are critical not only for synaptic pruning during CNS development, but also for new synaptic growth and basic synaptic neuroplasticity among mature neurons. Finally, molecular mechanisms by which microglia and neurons communicate to each other to coordinate synaptic remodeling actions are reviewed. The experiments discussed in Section 4 reveal that the neurons of brains that lack microglia are impaired in their ability to grow new spines during learning, lapse in normal spine turnover during development, develop larger arborizations with a preponderance of weak excitatory synapses due to failures of pruning, and show impaired functional connectivity between sections of tissue. This review aims to discuss the various mechanisms that govern the interaction between microglia and neurons, from the molecular to the organ system level, and to highlight the importance of these interactions in the development, maintenance, and pathogenesis of the CNS. Recent research has revealed that microglia-neuron interaction is vital for regulating fundamental neuronal functions, such as synaptic pruning, axonal remodeling, and neurogenesis. * ### Dysfunctional synaptic pruning by microglia correlates with cognitive impairment in sleep-deprived mice: Involvement of CX3CR1 signaling. The CX3C motif chemokine fractalkine receptor (CX3CR1), exclusively expressed on microglia in the central nervous system (CNS), is an eat-me signal-related protein and is responsible for synapse elimination (Lee and Chung, 2019; Paolicelli et al., 2011). Downregulation of CX3CR1 alters the synaptic pruning of microglia and increases spines in the dentate gyrus (Fernández de Cossío et al., 2017).

results.title: Receptor-receptor interactions and microvesicle exchange as mechanisms modulating signaling between neurons and astrocytes - ScienceDirect
results.content: ## Neuropharmacology. Volume 231, 15 June 2023, 109509. # Receptor-receptor interactions and microvesicle exchange as mechanisms modulating signaling between neurons and astrocytes. Author links open overlay panel, , , , ,. Under a Creative Commons license. ## Highlights. A bidirectional exchange of signals occurs between neurons and astrocytes. In both cells, the recognition of this pattern of signals is mediated by receptors. Receptors are also involved in mechanisms tuning the intercellular cross-talk. The formation of receptor complexes at the cell membrane is a first mechanism. A further mechanism is the transfer of receptors via extracellular microvesicles. ## Abstract. It is well known that astrocytes play a significant metabolic role in the nervous tissue, maintaining the homeostasis of the extracellular space and of the blood-brain barrier, and providing trophic support to neurons. In addition, however, evidence exists indicating astrocytes as important elements for brain activity through signaling exchange with neurons. Astrocytes, indeed, can sense synaptic activity and their molecular machinery responds to neurotransmitters released by neurons with cytoplasmic Ca2+ elevations that, in turn, stimulate the release of neuroactive substances (gliotransmitters) influencing nearby neurons. In both cell types the recognition and transduction of this complex pattern of signals is mediated by specific receptors that are also involved in mechanisms tuning the intercellular cross-talk between astrocytes and neurons. Two of these mechanisms are the focus of the present discussion. The first concerns direct receptor-receptor interactions leading to the formation at the cell membrane of multimeric receptor complexes. The cooperativity that emerges in the actions of orthosteric and allosteric ligands of the monomers forming the assembly provides the cell decoding apparatus with sophisticated and flexible dynamics in terms of recognition and signal transduction pathways. A further mechanism of plasticity involving receptors is based on the transfer of elements of the cellular signaling apparatus via extracellular microvesicles acting as protective containers, which can lead to transient changes in the transmitting/decoding capabilities of the target cell. This article is part of the Special Issue on “The receptor-receptor interaction as a new target for therapy”. ## Graphical abstract. ## Keywords. ## Data availability.
